Two clues, and together they pin the answer down.
Clue 1 — the oxidation product reacts with phenylhydrazine. Phenylhydrazine condenses with a
carbonyl group, so the product is an aldehyde or a ketone.
Clue 2 — it does *not* give the silver mirror test. Tollens' reagent is reduced by aldehydes but
not by ketones, so the product must be a ketone.
A ketone is produced by oxidising a **secondary** alcohol.
Now check the options. Ethanol (3) is primary and would give ethanal, which does give a silver
mirror. Ethanal (2) is already the aldehyde. Propane (4) is not oxidised by K₂Cr₂O₇ at all.
2-Propanol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, is secondary:
CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ --[O]--> CH₃COCH₃ (propanone), a ketone ✓
∴ X is 2-propanol.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|24||0|0.s:
Follow each reagent.
CH₃COOH + PCl₅ — the –OH of the acid is replaced by chlorine:
A = CH₃COCl, acetyl chloride.
A + C₆H₆ with anhydrous AlCl₃ — Friedel–Crafts acylation. The acylium ion CH₃CO⁺ substitutes
onto the ring:
B = C₆H₅COCH₃, acetophenone.
B + CH₃MgBr — a Grignard adds across the C=O. The carbanion-like CH₃⁻ attacks the carbonyl
carbon and the alkoxide is protonated on work-up.
The carbonyl carbon of acetophenone already carries a CH₃ and a C₆H₅; adding one more CH₃
and an OH gives a carbon bearing three carbon groups and an OH — a tertiary alcohol:
C = (CH₃)₂C(OH)C₆H₅, 2-phenylpropan-2-ol.
∴ (CH₃)₂C(OH)C₆H₅.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|25||0|0.s:
Convert mass to moles, then moles to atoms.
Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 2(16) = 44 g mol⁻¹
moles of CO₂ = 4.4 / 44 = 0.1 mol
Each CO₂ molecule contains 2 oxygen atoms, so
moles of O atoms = 0.1 × 2 = 0.2 mol
Number of O atoms = 0.2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.2044 × 10²³
The trap is option (2), 6 × 10²², which is the answer if you forget there are two oxygens per
molecule, and option (3), which is the count of *molecules* times ten.
∴ about 1.2 × 10²³ oxygen atoms.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|26||0|0.s:
Bond enthalpies give ΔH as (energy to break the reactant bonds) − (energy released forming
the product bonds).
Reaction: H₂(g) + Br₂(g) ⇒ 2HBr(g)
Bonds broken: one H–H and one Br–Br
= 433 + 192 = 625 kJ (absorbed, positive)
Bonds formed: two H–Br
= 2 × 364 = 728 kJ (released, negative)
ΔH° = 625 − 728 = −103 kJ
The negative sign says more energy comes out forming the two H–Br bonds than goes in breaking
the two reactant bonds, so the reaction is exothermic ✓
∴ ΔH° = −103 kJ.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|27||0|0.s:
Write the solubility product for the equilibrium:
Fe(OH)₃(s) ⇌ Fe³⁺ + 3OH⁻
Ksp = [Fe³⁺][OH⁻]³
The solid does not appear in the expression, and Ksp is a constant at fixed temperature, so the
product [Fe³⁺][OH⁻]³ cannot change.
Let the hydroxide fall to a quarter: [OH⁻]new = ¼[OH⁻]
Then [OH⁻]new³ = (¼)³[OH⁻]³ = (1/64)[OH⁻]³
To keep the product constant, [Fe³⁺] must rise by the reciprocal:
[Fe³⁺]new = 64 × [Fe³⁺]
Note the cube — the stoichiometric coefficient becomes the exponent, which is why a modest
change in OH⁻ has such a large effect.
∴ 64 times.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|28||0|0:
This is the third law of thermodynamics, and the wording has to be exact.
The law states: the entropy of a **perfectly crystalline solid** is zero at absolute zero.
The reason is statistical. Entropy measures the number of ways the particles can be arranged,
S = k ln W. In a perfect crystal at 0 K every particle is in its fixed lattice position and every
motion has ceased, so there is exactly one possible arrangement: W = 1, ln 1 = 0, hence S = 0.
Now test the options against that wording.
(2) says +ve — wrong, it is exactly zero.
(3) says *all* crystalline substances — wrong, only perfect ones. A crystal with defects, or one
with residual disorder such as CO, keeps a residual entropy at 0 K.
(4) says 0 °C — wrong, that is 273 K, not absolute zero.
∴ at absolute zero the entropy of a perfectly crystalline solid is zero.
kcet|Chemistry|2016|31||0|0:
Copper matte is the intermediate produced when copper pyrites, CuFeS₂, is smelted.
The ore is first roasted, which partly oxidises the iron, and then smelted with silica in a
reverberatory furnace. The silica is there to remove the iron oxide as slag:
FeO + SiO₂ ⇒ FeSiO₃ (slag, which floats off)
What is left as a separate molten layer is the matte, and it is still a mixture of sulphides:
mainly Cu₂S with some FeS remaining.
The matte is then transferred to a Bessemer converter, where a blast of air finishes the job:
2Cu₂S + 3O₂ ⇒ 2Cu₂O + 2SO₂, then 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S ⇒ 6Cu + SO₂
That last self-reduction gives blister copper.
∴ copper matte is Cu₂S + FeS.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|32||0|0.s:
This is the Bayer process for purifying bauxite.
Bauxite is Al₂O₃ contaminated with Fe₂O₃, SiO₂ and TiO₂. The separation works because Al₂O₃
is amphoteric while the iron and titanium oxides are basic.
Treating with hot concentrated NaOH dissolves only the alumina:
Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O ⇒ 2Na[Al(OH)₄]
The aluminium leaves as the soluble tetrahydroxoaluminate complex, in which Al(III) is
four-coordinate with four OH⁻ ligands and the sodium is the counter ion.
The insoluble impurities are filtered off as red mud.
The solution is then seeded with fresh Al(OH)₃ to precipitate the hydroxide, which is heated to
give pure Al₂O₃ for electrolysis.
∴ Na[Al(OH)₄].

kcet|Chemistry|2016|33||0|0.s:
Find the statement that is false.
(1) True — fluorine's reactions are strongly exothermic, because the bonds it forms are very
strong and its own bond is weak.
(2) True — fluorine forms only one oxoacid, HOF (hypofluorous acid). The other halogens form
several, because they can expand their octet using d orbitals; fluorine, in period 2, cannot.
(3) True — fluorine is the most electronegative element, 4.0 on the Pauling scale.
(4) False — the F–F bond enthalpy is unusually **low**, about 158 kJ mol⁻¹, lower even than
Cl–Cl at 242. The two fluorine atoms are so small that their non-bonding lone pairs are forced
close together and repel strongly, weakening the bond.
That weak bond is precisely why statement (1) is true: little energy is needed to start the
reaction and a great deal is released.
∴ statement (4) is not true.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|34||0|0.s:
Check each claim about nitrogen against its neighbours in group 15.
(1) Less electronegative — false. Nitrogen is the *most* electronegative of the group, 3.0.
(2) Low ionisation enthalpy — false. Its small size and half-filled 2p³ configuration give it an
unusually *high* ionisation enthalpy.
(3) d orbitals available — false. Nitrogen is a second period element, so it has only 2s and 2p.
This is exactly why its covalency never exceeds four, while phosphorus reaches five in PCl₅.
(4) True — nitrogen is small enough for its 2p orbitals to overlap sideways effectively, so it
forms pπ–pπ multiple bonds with itself. The result is N≡N, with a bond enthalpy of 941 kJ mol⁻¹,
which is why nitrogen is a diatomic gas and so unreactive.
Phosphorus, being larger, cannot do this and instead exists as P₄ with single bonds.
∴ its ability to form pπ–pπ bonds with itself.
